title: Which kind of database fits you?

questions.q: Do you know your main lookups today?
questions.hint: For example, "get this user's cart by user ID".

options.label: No, our questions will keep changing
Yes, a few fixed lookups
options.why: NoSQL is efficient for lookups you plan in advance

questions.q: Must several records change together or not at all?

options.label: Yes, like orders and payments
options.why: transactions are a core SQL feature, and NoSQL ones come with limits

options.label: Not really
options.why: you can skip the transaction limits

questions.q: How big could your writes get?

options.label: One server should cope
options.why: a basic setup with one main server is simpler

options.label: More than one server can take
options.why: these are built to spread writes over many servers

questions.q: What does your data look like?

options.label: Clear links, like customers and orders
options.why: tables with joins fit related data

options.label: Fields vary a lot from record to record
options.why: documents hold varied shapes, and jsonb helps SQL too

options.label: My team already knows SQL
options.why: you can use skills you already have

options.label: I want a service to handle the servers
options.why: A managed service handles the servers for you

options.label: We can run a distributed system
options.why: scaling out adds infrastructure and upkeep

questions.q: Do reads need to see the latest write every time?

options.label: Yes, always
options.why: strict guarantees are what relational databases are built around

options.label: I would like to tune it per use
options.why: Cassandra lets you set how many copies must answer

sql.name: SQL (relational)
sql.summary: Tables of related rows, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, where you can join anything later.
sql.bestWhen: Your data has clear relationships, several records must change together, or you do not yet know every question you will ask.
sql.watchOut: Schema changes need care, and a very high write rate pushes you toward harder setups.

document.name: Document database
document.summary: JSON-like documents, such as MongoDB or Couchbase, for nested data and varied shapes.
document.bestWhen: Records vary a lot in shape and you want to keep related data together in one document.
document.watchOut: Many cross-collection joins are weak spots, and with no enforced shape, mistakes move into your code.

keyvalue.name: Key-value store
keyvalue.summary: One value per unique key, such as DynamoDB or Redis, for fast reads and writes.
keyvalue.bestWhen: You look up a record by key at huge scale and want the service to handle servers for you.
keyvalue.watchOut: Questions other than "get by key" can be slow and costly, and DynamoDB transactions have size and Region limits.

widecolumn.name: Wide-column database
widecolumn.summary: Flexible columns per row, such as Cassandra or HBase, built to add nodes as you grow.
widecolumn.bestWhen: You have a large write stream, predictable query patterns and a team that can run a distributed system.
widecolumn.watchOut: Ad hoc questions are hard, and you take on a distributed system with its tuning and failure cases.
